Two years after the CFMEU collapsed into chaos, the man charged with investigating its worst branch says a royal commission is still necessary.

The anger rises then recedes. Typically warm and candid, Geoffrey Watson’s wry bemusement with public criticism can sour if he believes the criticism impugns his integrity. So it was in our lengthy conversation this week.

In February, a report prepared by Watson, a silk and former counsel assisting the New South Wales Independent Commission Against Corruption, was released and a mighty storm ensued. Appointed in 2024 by the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union’s then administrator, Mark Irving, to examine the union’s corruption, Watson delivered a 140-page investigation of the Victorian branch, which he titled “Rotting from the Top”.

The report collected evidence of graft, intimidation and the influence of organised crime upon the state’s construction sector – especially within the massive, state-sponsored infrastructure projects known as the Big Build.

“As a lifelong believer in trade unions, it was shocking to see so much crime, so much corruption, such a perversion of values,” Watson wrote. “The CFMEU was no longer on the right side of civil society, it was proudly on the wrong side. The Union was no longer the champion of the working class – the Setka era CFMEU turned to looking after gangsters, standover men, bikies, heroin traffickers, and even killers. By the end of this investigation I have been left with the empty feeling that the Setka-led Victorian branch of the CFMEU was no longer a trade union, it was a crime syndicate.”

Provocatively, Watson also asserted that the scale of corruption was partly helped by political indifference – a kind of wilful blindness. This view was removed from the final draft, a fact we learnt when news of the omissions leaked and lawyers, their curiosity aroused, had the cut sections tabled during Queensland’s commission of inquiry into that state’s branch of the CFMEU.

“It’s appropriate that politicians and public servants should share the responsibility for what has happened – for allowing the CFMEU to run out of control,” Watson wrote. “It is not as though the excesses of the CFMEU have been a secret: the CFMEU revelled in bad publicity … If the press knew, then the public knew. If the public knew, then the Government must have known. More to the point, as the guardian of public money, the Government had a duty to know. It had a duty to monitor delays and costs-blowouts. There is no doubt the Government knew about the rising problem – but it is equally clear that the Government did nothing about it.”

For days after, Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan, who was the state’s infrastructure minister before her promotion three years ago, quivered with indignation. Testy media conferences followed. Allan zeroed in on a figure Watson has used – an estimate, as he qualifies in his report, that the cost of Big Build corruption was likely about $15 billion. The specificity of this figure, and Mark Irving’s private querying of it, had the unfortunate consequence of distracting from the wider findings by offering critics a number to quibble over and use to invite suspicion of Watson’s reliability. “That claim, of any amount, has not been well tested or properly founded,” Allan said in February.

Her police minister, Anthony Carbines, went much further in his criticisms of Watson. “It might be good for a quote, but he’s not much good when it comes to coming up with some facts,” he said. “When his florid ramblings become facts that can be tested in court, all well and good. But if you’ve got evidence, give it to Victoria Police and they’ll take action.”

Watson says he was often in contact with Victoria Police during his investigations – that of course he was – and notes of anger sound when he thinks again of Carbines’ comments. At the time, Watson described the remarks as “Trumpian”, and this week it was made clear that the insult to his integrity still stings.

It was an unusual and unpleasant moment for Watson. His report had attracted the ire of both the Victorian government and the alleged underworld figures and allegedly corrupt former union officials named in it. For a time, they all were joined by the similarity of their denunciations of Watson. Lawsuits have followed, of which Watson cannot speak. “I think Geoffrey would have needed a thorough shower after those years of investigating this putrid mess,” one union source told The Saturday Paper this week. “And they’re still attacking him.”

Watson says he had not appreciated the scale of corruption in Victoria before he began investigating the union in 2024. Then again, why would he? He was a Sydney silk, ordinarily engaged with the prosecution of bent coppers and politicians in that state. “I wondered going into it if it was all a beat-up,” he says. “But on a scale of zero to 10 for corruption, NSW was a two or three. Queensland a five. Victoria was a 1000. Insane. There was trafficking of heroin on sites – and meth, coke. Bikie gangs were fighting each other for control of these sites.”

“I think Geoffrey would have needed a thorough shower after those years of investigating this putrid mess. And they’re still attacking him.”

There’s only one thing for it, Watson says, and his view was echoed by several union sources this week: a royal commission, or something similar, as was instated in Queensland. “If you really want to get to the bottom of all this, then you need a properly empowered public inquiry in the nature of a royal commission,” he says.

Labor’s Big Build, and its entanglement with union corruption and organised crime, will inevitably be invoked in the Victorian election campaign this year. The state will vote in November, when Labor will seek a fourth consecutive term. Union sources are not holding their breath for an inquiry, as proposed by Watson. Allan has made clear that she feels it unnecessary. “There’s no  way the Allan government would call one,” a union source says. “But a commission of inquiry, as happened in Queensland, is what’s needed. Only a serious, independent inquiry will do it.”

In January, the CFMEU’s national secretary, Zach Smith, abruptly resigned. “The reasons I am leaving are personal,” he wrote in a statement. “I cannot continue to serve the union in the way that the members deserve, and taking time away is in the best interests of myself, the people I care about and the union.”

What wasn’t revealed at that time was that he was being investigated by his boss, Mark Irving, for alleged undeclared conflicts of interest regarding romantic relationships with staff.

Irving inherited Smith. The union boss was someone viewed with contemptuous suspicion by whistleblowers within the CFMEU, given his previous closeness to expelled leader John Setka. Nonetheless, Irving was patient with Smith and forgave several missteps – such as when Smith directed a union official to meet with the notorious underworld figure Mick Gatto last year.

Yet Smith’s romantic entanglements, and his less-than-forthcoming disclosures of them and their subsequent conflicts of interest, made his time there untenable. Irving felt personally betrayed, as did many others within the union, who had received from Smith misleading assurances.

Then, in April, Irving resigned. “The Union is changing its personnel,” he said. “It is changing its culture. It is regaining its position in civil society. The rebuild phase requires a different approach … and a different set of skills.”

This was less of a surprise than Smith’s departure. Irving had received a “hospital pass”, in the words of one union source, and inherited a complex and potentially dangerous job. He suffered a heart attack last year and had subsequent surgery, and from early in his tenure was the recipient of several credible death threats. This obliged the deployment of personal security. Sources have told me how Irving learnt to choose tables in restaurants and cafes that provided clear sightlines to the door. “The threats were very, very serious,” one source says. “These were serious people.”

Geoffrey Watson is happy to concede that in his time as corruption investigator, there were disagreements with Irving. They were “always civil”, he says, and not for the first time he stresses Irving’s decency.

“It’s difficult to overstate the difficulty of his job,” Watson says. “And he was earning much less money than he would at the bar. I have great respect for him.”

Nonetheless, in the almost two years of the CFMEU’s government mandated administration, there has been significant staff tumult. Poor appointments were made of people facing serious allegations, who were then sacked or offered generous severance packages, and the departure of Smith means that in under two years the Victorian branch has had four different leaders.

There has been attrition in the administrator’s office also – not only Irving’s departure but also several support staff. None of this surprises one whistleblower. “Look, a lot of Labor or ACTU associated unionists came in to fix the problem,” they say. “But construction is an entirely different culture. They were outsiders to this: people plucked from outside the culture and then dropped into maximum security.”

Irving has been replaced by Michael Crosby, a veteran unionist and former executive of the CFMEU’s NSW branch. Even among the most militant and impatient agitators for reform within the union, there’s begrudging respect for his reputation for integrity and a willingness to confer some benefit of doubt. That said, there remains scepticism of the appointment of another man with very little experience in construction.

“The next phase” begins, as Mark Irving said, but union sources told me they have no idea what that means. Irving did oversee the dismissal of hundreds of people, but many of those departures came with generous severance packages – a fact that angers whistleblowers, not least those who have suffered from their blacklisting for speaking out.

“After almost two years of administration, what’s the scorecard?” asks one union source. “There’s not much. We’ve had some clowns appointed to positions, which turned bad. We’ve had huge payouts to some folks. And how many charges? How many people are feeling the serious blowtorch of criminal charges?

“The goal is to clean up this union and return it in a fit state to members – who can then hold democratic elections for leadership positions. But honestly, almost two years later, we’ve never felt further away from that.”

Martin McKenzie-Murray is The Saturday Paper’s associate editor.
